title: Reproducible service dependency declarations · Python package organization for a service

blocks.text: A teammate needs committed dependency declarations, not a memory of local installation steps.
python -m pip freeze reports installed packages and versions. Save that output to requirements.txt as a dependency declaration.
Install with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. Reconstruct from committed declarations, not manually installed packages elsewhere; the build stage obtains the declared dependencies.

blocks.text: Inspect versions with python -m pip freeze, save requirements.txt and commit the declaration. Install from it in the environment being reconstructed. Compare declared packages with those obtained for the build. A local installation is not the handoff contract, and freeze alone does not reproduce every external service condition.
One successful run in a manually prepared environment is not a dependency declaration. Reconstruct from the committed declaration.

segments.label: Save installed dependencies to requirements.txt
segments.summary: The demonstration creates and activates an isolated Python environment, installs example packages, and redirects pip freeze output into requirements.txt. The resulting declaration includes dependencies of the explicitly installed packages, which explains the additional entries. Sharing this file lets another person install the listed dependencies in their own environment.

blocks.group_title: Capture dependencies for a reproducible handoff

bridge.before: Watch how installed packages become a requirements.txt declaration. The clip uses bare pip in an activated environment; Devspace uses python -m pip to explicitly select the environment's Python interpreter.
bridge.after: The clip explains sharing the declaration, but omits the install -r command and committed-declaration build workflow. The text supplies both: install from requirements.txt and have the build obtain committed dependencies.

steps.eyebrow: Python package organization for a service
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Qualified names show which package owns a service module.
Packages organize modules as package.module. Regular packages contain __init__.py.
Use absolute package-qualified imports or relative imports with leading dots interpreted in the current package. Run in package context with python -m package.module; __name__ then becomes __main__.

blocks.code:
# Regular package marker: service/__init__.py (empty)
# Service module: service/orders.py
import service.orders
# In package context, leading-dot imports use the current package.
# Run from the shell: python -m service.orders
# Execution name: __main__

annotations.text: Regular package marker and module location.
Qualified identity versus package-relative import context.
Run in package context; distinguish qualified identity from execution name.

steps.eyebrow: Python package organization for a service
steps.title: Reason through an example

blocks.text: With service/__init__.py and service/orders.py, the qualified module is service.orders. An absolute import names the package; leading-dot imports depend on that package context. python -m service.orders runs it in package context with __name__ equal to __main__. Import identity and execution name serve different roles.
Relative imports depend on the current package. File location alone does not explain a leading dot.

public.prompt: Complete # PACKAGE comment entries. Supply the empty regular-package marker path, empty orders module path, qualified import name, package-context execution command, and execution name. For relative_context select current_package or working_directory to identify what leading dots mean. The unchanged harness creates the empty files at the supplied paths, imports the module and executes it with the same package context as -m. This player runs the supplied Python filesystem checker, not a shell command. Do not edit the checker. Edit only the six `# PACKAGE` entries. Leave all `# PY` lines and the supplied compiler unchanged.
